title: Money and paperwork
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: IMPERSONAL se says a thing is done without saying by whom, which is exactly what a sign and a counter clerk both want: aquí se paga en efectivo, no se puede fumar, ¿dónde se firma? L2-M4 opened the bare se for the street sense; this is the same word shown at length. The written twin, the passive with ser, is L4's business and appears nowhere here.

This module speaks USTED from the first word to the last, because a counter is the place the register decision was made for. The usted imperative L2-M1 opened is spent here: perdone, disculpe, firme, rellene, espere. For an -ar verb that cell ends in -e.

Three ways to attach money to time, and they are not swappable. para el lunes is a DEADLINE — the thing is due by then. antes del sábado is a LIMIT — before that point. por adelantado is a MANNER — how you pay, not when. It is L3-M2's para/por split doing its second shift.
del is de + el contracted, exactly as al is a + el. Spanish never writes de el, and the contraction happens only with el — de la, de los and de las stay apart.

The vocabulary here is what is printed on the actual paper rather than what a textbook prefers: alquiler, factura, recibo, plazo, formulario, sello, documento. Where a region says something else — el ticket, la boleta — the word's own note says so.

sentences.cue: Excuse me, where do I sign?

words.note: ¿Dónde se firma? asks where the signing happens, which is lighter on a clerk than asking where YOU should sign.

sentences.trap: Spanish does not put you in the question at all. ¿Dónde firmo? is possible but blunter; se firma asks about the process.
sentences.usage: usted, at a counter, from the first word. perdone is the usted form L2-M1 taught; perdona would be a friend.

words.note: Impersonal se with pagar, and indexed whole so L2-M4's bare se keeps its own row. aquí se paga en efectivo is what a sign says, not a person.
Cash, and it lives in the frame en efectivo. dinero is money in general; this is notes and coins crossing a counter.

sentences.trap: This is a sign, not a person. No subject exists to look for — se is the whole of who does it.

mistake.why: That points at one customer and reads as an order. A sign speaks to everyone: aquí se paga en efectivo.

sentences.usage: Printed on a card by a till. The module speaks usted, and an impersonal sign is the register at its most neutral.

sentences.cue: Can the rent be paid here?

words.note: Can, with nobody named. ¿Se puede? alone is may I come in; no se puede is a sign refusing flatly, and neither says who.
To pay, and what you pay takes no preposition at all: pago el alquiler. pagar por exists but only for an exchange — what you paid FOR something.
The rent, masculine: el alquiler. It is also the renting itself, which is why coche de alquiler is a hire car.

sentences.trap: se puede stays singular whatever follows it, and the second verb is an infinitive: se puede pagar, never se pueden pagar here.
sentences.usage: Asked across a counter, usted implied throughout. It is politer than ¿Puedo pagar aquí? because it asks about the rule, not about you.

sentences.display: Tengo que pagar el alquiler antes del sábado.
sentences.cue: I have to pay the rent before Saturday.
sentences.literal: I-have that to-pay the rent before of-the Saturday.

words.note: de + el contracted, exactly as al is a + el. Spanish never writes de el, and only el contracts — de la stays apart.

sentences.trap: de el is never written. The two words contract into del, and Spanish does it without asking.

mistake.display: Tengo que pagar el alquiler antes de el sábado.
mistake.why: The contraction is compulsory: antes del sábado. Only el contracts — antes de la reunión stays as it is.

sentences.usage: Said about your own obligation, so tengo que rather than hay que. usted is not needed when nobody is addressed.

sentences.display: Necesito el formulario, un documento y un sello.
sentences.cue: I need the form, an ID and a stamp.
sentences.literal: I-need the form, a document and a stamp.

words.note: The sheet you fill in, masculine: el formulario. La solicitud is the application it serves; this word is the paper itself.
Any document, and in Spain the ID card too: su documento, por favor. Its formal name is el DNI.
The office's rubber stamp on your form, and the postage kind as well. Without it a paper often does not count as handed in.

sentences.trap: documento is not the English document only — at a Spanish counter it is your ID card, and su documento means show it.
sentences.usage: What you say when you reach the window and want to know you have everything.

sentences.display: Rellene el formulario y firme aquí, por favor.
sentences.cue: Fill in the form and sign here, please.
sentences.literal: Fill-in the form and sign here, please.

words.note: usted imperative of rellenar, the paperwork verb. llenar alone is filling a glass; the re- is what makes it a form.
The usted imperative of firmar. An -ar verb takes -e for usted, which is why the cell looks like it belongs to another conjugation.

sentences.trap: Both verbs end in -e, and that -e is the usted imperative of an -ar verb. Rellena and firma would be tú, and out of place at a window.
sentences.sound: re-YE-ne in most of Spain, and re-JE-ne in Argentina; the ll carries the regional accent.
sentences.usage: What the clerk says to you, not what you say to the clerk. usted throughout, softened by por favor.

sentences.display: Espere un momento, aquí tiene el recibo.
sentences.cue: Wait a moment — here's your receipt.
sentences.literal: Wait a moment, here you-have the receipt.

words.note: usted imperative of the esperar L2 already taught. Espere un momento is the standard counter phrase and is not curt.
Proof that you paid, masculine: el recibo. In much of Latin America a shop slip is el ticket or la boleta instead.

sentences.trap: aquí tiene is the Spanish here you are, and it is a tiene, not a tenga: the clerk states, not commands.
sentences.usage: The counter's own two sentences, handed back to you. usted in both halves.

sentences.display: Tengo que entregar la factura antes del plazo.
sentences.cue: I have to hand in the bill before the deadline.
sentences.literal: I-have that to-hand-in the bill before of-the deadline.

words.note: To hand something over to whoever is meant to receive it. dar is merely giving; entregar carries the obligation with it.
The bill for a service — electricity, water, phone. A restaurant bill is la cuenta, which L2-M5 already taught; they are not interchangeable.
The stretch you are given, and so the deadline at the end of it. a plazos is the same word spread out: by instalments.

sentences.trap: factura is a service bill; la cuenta is a restaurant one. Asking for la factura at a table gets you the invoice for tax purposes.
sentences.usage: Said about your own deadline, in an office setting. The register stays formal because the setting does.

sentences.display: El alquiler es mil euros. Pago por adelantado.
sentences.cue: The rent is a thousand euros. I pay in advance.
sentences.literal: The rent is thousand euros. I-pay for advanced.

words.note: One thousand, and it never takes un in front: mil euros, not un mil euros. Counting, it does not go plural either.
The currency, kept lowercase in Spanish and written after the number: mil euros. The symbol usually follows too.
In advance, and por is doing its manner job here rather than para's forward-pointing one. It says HOW you pay, not when.

sentences.trap: No un before mil, and por rather than para: this is how the payment is made, not what it is aimed at.

mistake.display: El alquiler es un mil euros. Pago para adelantado.
mistake.why: mil stands alone, and advance payment is a manner, so por adelantado. para would point the money forward at a purpose.

sentences.usage: Stating your own terms to a landlord or an agency. Formal, because money is being named.

sentences.display: Necesito una cita previa en el banco.
sentences.cue: I need an appointment at the bank.
sentences.literal: I-need an appointment previous in the bank.

words.note: The phrase on the door of every Spanish office. cita on its own is any appointment, a date included, so previa is what makes it official.

sentences.trap: previa comes after the noun, as almost every Spanish adjective does. cita previa is a fixed pair and the two words are not separated.
sentences.usage: The phrase every office door carries, said back to the office. usted setting throughout.
sentences.mnemonic: cita previa: the appointment you needed before you needed the appointment.
